meaning: Expresses the speaker's guess: “I think ... probably”. Softer than 「だろう」 alone, and makes clear it's a personal view.
connection: Plain form (nouns and な-adjective stems attach directly) + だろうと思う

senses.label: I think ... probably
senses.meaning: A guess based on the situation, like “I think it'll probably ...”. Less certain than 「〜と思う」. Often used with 「たぶん」 or 「きっと」.
senses.connection: Verb / い-adjective plain form + だろうと思う; noun / な-adjective stem + だろうと思う
examples: I think it'll probably rain tomorrow.
I think this problem is probably hard even for him.
I think the area in front of the station is surely lively.

senses.label: Negative guess
senses.meaning: With a negative form, it means “I don't think ... will”. Japanese puts the negative inside the guessed clause rather than saying 「〜とは思わない」.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form + だろうと思う (「来ないだろうと思う」, 「間に合わないだろうと思う」)
examples: I don't think he'll come.
I don't think we'll make it even if we go now.

senses.label: What I guessed back then
senses.meaning: 「〜だろうと思った」 says you had that guess at the time. It often sounds like “I knew it” or “I thought so, but actually ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + だろうと思った／だろうと思っていた
examples: I thought so.
I thought it would be easy, but it was surprisingly hard.

notes: 「でしょう」 can't go before 「と思う」: ✕「雨が降るでしょうと思います」→ ○「雨が降るだろうと思います」. Politeness shows only at the end, in 「思います」.
Don't add 「だ」 after nouns or な-adjectives: ✕「学生だだろうと思う」 ✕「静かなだろうと思う」→ ○「学生だろうと思う」「静かだろうと思う」.
To report someone else's guess, plain 「と思う」 doesn't work: ✕「田中さんは雨が降るだろうと思う」→ ○「田中さんは雨が降るだろうと思っている」.
「〜だろうと思った」 on its own means “I knew it (just as I expected)”, but followed by 「が／のに」 it means “I thought ..., but it wasn't so”: the exact opposite. Check what comes next.
For “I don't think he'll come”, put the negative first: 「来ないだろうと思う」. Saying 「来るだろうとは思わない」 flatly rejects the other person's expectation and sounds harsh.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: A friend asks if you can go out this weekend, and you give your guess.
daily.example: I think it'll probably be sunny this weekend.

daily.title: Guessing someone's situation
daily.description: A friend hasn't replied, and you guess why.
daily.example: I think she's probably busy right now.

daily.title: Just as expected
daily.description: Said casually when things turn out the way you thought.
daily.example: Yep. I thought so.

work.title: Forecasts in a meeting
work.description: Telling your boss how the project is going, leaving some room for error.
work.example: I think this plan will probably be finished next month.

work.title: A personal judgment in a report
work.description: Writing your own forecast in a report or essay.
work.example: The number of users will probably keep growing.

etymology: 「だろう」 comes from 「であろう」: 「である」 plus the guessing auxiliary 「う」. Adding 「と思う」 (“I think”) marks the guess as the speaker's own opinion.
formation: Made of three parts: 「だろう」 + the quoting particle 「と」 + 「思う」. 「だろう」 is the conjectural form of the copula 「だ」 (from 「であろう」), meaning “probably is”; 「と」 wraps the whole guess before it like quotation marks; 「思う」 marks it as a thought in the speaker's mind. Together: “I present the guess ‘it's probably ...’ as my own thought.” That's why the subject is naturally “I”, and why it adds a cushion of “just my view” compared with plain 「だろう」, sounding softer. Since 「だろう」 already contains 「だ」, you can't add another 「だ」 after nouns or な-adjectives; for politeness only the final 「思います」 changes, never 「でしょう」.

similar.title: 〜だろう
similar.explanation: Same origin: this pattern is simply 「だろう」 + 「と思う」. 「だろう」 alone is a blunt guess, leaning toward casual male speech or writing; adding 「と思う」 frames the guess as “my view”, which sounds softer, and it can be made polite as 「〜だろうと思います」.

similar.title: 〜でしょう (guess / confirmation)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「でしょう」 is the polite form of 「だろう」 and states a guess directly to the listener, objectively, like a weather forecast; 「〜だろうと思います」 stresses that it's the speaker's personal guess. The two can't be stacked as ✕「でしょうと思います」.

similar.title: 〜と思う (I think)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜と思う」 states opinions and judgments with fairly high confidence (「彼は来ると思う」); inserting 「だろう」 turns it into a pure guess with less certainty (「彼は来るだろうと思う」).

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「かもしれない」 means “maybe, might”: it only says something is possible, with about a 50% chance or less; 「だろうと思う」 means the speaker thinks it's quite likely.

meaning: Talks about a fixed plan or schedule. More objective than 「つもり」; usually something already decided.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ない-form + 予定だ; noun + の + 予定だ

senses.label: A set plan
senses.meaning: Says something is scheduled to happen. It sounds objective and is used for arrangements that are unlikely to change, like “be scheduled to ...”, “plan to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + 予定だ／予定です (negative: verb ない-form + 予定だ)
examples: I'm planning to go to Japan next month.
The meeting is scheduled to start at three.
I'm not planning to go back home this year.

senses.label: Noun + の予定
senses.meaning: After a noun, 「の予定」 shows that something is on the schedule. 予定 also works as a plain noun: 「予定がある」 “I have plans”.
senses.connection: Noun + の予定だ (「出張の予定」, 「旅行の予定」)
examples: I'm scheduled to go on a business trip tomorrow.
Have you decided on your weekend plans yet?

senses.label: The original plan
senses.meaning: 「〜予定だった」 talks about what was planned, usually hinting that it didn't happen. Often followed by 「が」 or 「けど」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + 予定だった + が／けど／のに
examples: I was supposed to meet a friend yesterday, but it was called off because of the rain.
I was supposed to arrive at eight, but the train was late.

notes: 「予定です」 means it's already settled. Saying it about something undecided will be taken at face value (say 「来年結婚する予定です」 and people may congratulate you). For something that's only an idea, use 「〜たいと思っています」 or 「〜(よ)うと思っています」.
Don't use 「つもり」 to ask about a superior's or client's plans: ✕「部長は明日どうするつもりですか」 sounds like an interrogation; ○「明日のご予定はいかがですか」.
「〜予定でした」 usually implies the plan fell through, and listeners will understand “but it didn't happen”. If things went as planned, say 「予定通り〜ました」.
Attach verbs in the dictionary form or ない-form, not the ます-form: ✕「行きます予定です」→ ○「行く予定です」. Nouns take 「の」: 「出張の予定です」.

daily.title: Summer vacation plans
daily.description: A friend asks about your summer break, and you explain what's already set.
daily.example: I'm planning to go to Okinawa with my family over summer vacation.

daily.title: Making plans with a friend
daily.description: Asking if someone is free on a certain day.
daily.example: Got any plans on Saturday?

daily.title: Plans falling through
daily.description: Complaining that your plans didn't work out.
daily.example: I was going to go shopping today, but I came down with a fever.

work.title: Telling a client the schedule
work.description: In a business email, giving the planned delivery or meeting date.
work.example: The item is scheduled to ship next Monday.

work.title: News and announcements
work.description: A news report or notice about an upcoming event.
work.example: The new station is scheduled to open next spring.

etymology: 「予定」 is a Sino-Japanese word: 「予」 means “in advance” and 「定」 means “decide”, so it's “something decided in advance”. As a noun followed by 「だ／です」, it forms “be scheduled to ...”.
formation: 「予定」 is a Sino-Japanese noun: 「予」 = “in advance”, 「定」 = “fix, set”, so “something fixed in advance”. The verb clause before it modifies this noun (「日本へ行く＋予定」), and the copula 「だ／です」 follows, literally “(this) is the pre-arranged ‘going to Japan’”. That's why verbs take the dictionary or ない-form, which can modify nouns, and nouns connect with 「の」. The whole sentence is basically a noun-predicate statement about a fact on the schedule, not a wish in your heart, so it sounds objective and the subject can even be a meeting or a train. In the past, 「予定だった」 means “what was originally arranged was ...”, which naturally suggests things didn't go as planned.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「つもり」 is the speaker's subjective intention, not necessarily arranged yet; 「予定」 is something already on the schedule and more objective, and it can even have non-human subjects such as meetings or trains (「電車は九時に着く予定です」, not ✕「着くつもりです」).

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜(よ)うと思う」 is an intention in your mind right now, perhaps just decided; 「予定だ」 is something already arranged.

similar.title: 〜ことになっている
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「ことになっている」 stresses an arrangement decided by rules, the company or other people that you have to follow; 「予定だ」 just states what's on the schedule, regardless of who decided it.

meaning: 「AはBほど〜ない」 means “A is not as ... as B”, a negative comparison.
connection: Noun / verb plain form + ほど + negative predicate

senses.label: A is not as ... as B
senses.meaning: Uses B as the standard and says A doesn't reach that level, like “A is not as ... as B”. The predicate must be negative.
senses.connection: AはBほど + い-adjective く／な-adjective で + ない (ありません)
examples: This summer isn't as hot as last year.
I'm not as tall as my older brother.
This restaurant isn't as expensive as the one in front of the station.

senses.label: Not that ...
senses.meaning: 「それほど〜ない」 means “not that ...”, and 「思ったほど〜ない」 means “not as ... as I thought”. The degree is lower than expected.
senses.connection: それほど／思ったほど／言うほど + negative form
examples: Japanese isn't that difficult.
This test wasn't as hard as I thought.

senses.label: Not bad enough to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ほどではない」 says something hasn't reached a certain level, like “it's not so bad that ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / noun + ほどではない
examples: It's a bit cold, but not cold enough for a coat.
The injury wasn't bad enough to need a hospital stay.

notes: 「ほど」 must be followed by a negative; for positive comparisons use 「より」: ✕「兄は私ほど背が高い」→ ○「兄は私より背が高い」.

Swapping A and B reverses the meaning: 「兄は私ほど背が高くない」 means “my brother isn't as tall as me” (I'm taller), not “I'm not as tall as my brother”. The noun before 「ほど」 is the one with more of the quality.
「AはBほど〜ない」 (A isn't as ... as B) and 「BほどAはない」 (nothing is more A than B; B is the best) look alike but mean completely different things: 「東京ほど便利な町はない」 praises Tokyo as the most convenient city.

Commenting on a meal someone treated you to, or on a gift, with 「思ったほどおいしくなかった」 sounds disappointed and very rude. On the other hand, 「それほどでもないです」 is a graceful, modest reply when asked whether something was hard.

daily.title: Comparing the weather
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about today and yesterday.
daily.example: It's not as cold today as yesterday, huh.

daily.title: How your studies are going
daily.description: Answering modestly when asked if Japanese is hard.
daily.example: Kanji wasn't as hard as I thought.

daily.title: Feeling a little unwell
daily.description: Reassuring a worried family member that it's not serious.
daily.example: I'm fine. It's not bad enough to see a doctor.

work.title: Analyzing numbers
work.description: Comparing two months of sales in a meeting.
work.example: Sales this month haven't grown as much as last month.

work.title: News reports
work.description: Comparing the impact of a storm or disaster.
work.example: This typhoon didn't cause as much damage as the last one.

etymology: 「ほど」 is written 「程」 and originally meant “degree, limit”. 「Bほど」 is “to the degree of B”; with a negative, it becomes “not reaching B's level”.
formation: 「ほど」 was originally the noun 「程」, “degree, limit”. 「Bほど」 means “B's degree”, setting B up as a yardstick; followed by a negative 「〜ない」, it means “doesn't reach the B yardstick”, i.e. “A isn't as ... as B”. Since B is the yardstick, B must be the one with more of the quality; and since the sentence is about whether the yardstick is reached, it only works with a negative, so positive comparisons switch to 「より」. 「それほど」 and 「思ったほど」 simply replace the yardstick with “that degree” or “the degree I imagined”, giving “not that ...” and “not as ... as I thought”.

similar.title: 〜ほど (degree)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「ほど（程）」 for degree. 「〜ほど」 alone uses an example as a yardstick for a high degree and can be positive (「泣きたいほど痛い」); this pattern means “doesn't reach B's level” and must pair with a negative.

similar.title: 〜ほど〜はない
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「BほどAはない」 puts 「は」 after the noun and ends with 「ない」, meaning “nothing is more A than B”, a superlative; this pattern, 「AはBほど〜ない」, only says A falls short of B. A small change in word order, a completely different meaning.

similar.title: 〜は〜より〜 (comparison)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「AはBより〜」 is a neutral comparison and can be positive or negative; 「AはBほど〜ない」 specifically says “A doesn't reach B's level”, sounds gentler, and is often used to soften an evaluation.

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: the same fact can be told from either side: 「私は兄ほど背が高くない」 = 「私より兄のほうが背が高い」. The first takes A as the topic and says “A isn't as ... as B”; the second says directly “B is more ...”.

meaning: As one thing increases, the other changes with it: “the more ..., the more ...”.
connection: Verb ば-form + same verb dictionary form + ほど; い-adjective ければ + い-adjective + ほど; な-adjective なら + な-adjective な + ほど

senses.label: Verbs: the more you do it ...
senses.meaning: The same verb is repeated. The more you do the action, the stronger the result: “the more ..., the more ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ば-form + verb dictionary form + ほど (「すればするほど」, 「考えれば考えるほど」)
examples: The more you study Japanese, the more interesting it gets.
The more I thought about it, the less I understood.
The more of this soup I drink, the better it tastes.

senses.label: Adjectives: the more ..., the more ...
senses.meaning: The same adjective is repeated. The more of that quality, the more the second part applies.
senses.connection: い-adjective ければ + い-adjective + ほど; な-adjective なら + な-adjective な + ほど
examples: The fresher vegetables are, the better they taste.
The bigger the room, the better.
The simpler the explanation, the better.

notes: Adjective forms are the most common mistake: 「いい」 becomes 「よければよいほど」 (✕「いいければいいほど」); な-adjectives use 「なら〜なほど」: ✕「簡単ければ簡単なほど」→ ○「簡単なら簡単なほど」.
The ば-form comes first and the dictionary form second, never the other way round: ✕「考えるほど考えれば」→ ○「考えれば考えるほど」.
The second part must be a state or evaluation that can rise or fall along with the first, not a one-time event: ✕「練習すればするほど、試合に勝った」→ ○「練習すればするほど、上手になる」.
Telling a superior or client 「早ければ早いほどいいです」 amounts to pressuring them and sounds pushy; in business say 「お早めにご対応いただけますと幸いです」.

daily.title: Learning a language
daily.description: Telling a friend how studying Japanese feels.
daily.example: The more you practice, the better you get.

daily.title: Shopping
daily.description: Saying what you want when choosing a product.
daily.example: For a laptop, the lighter the better.

daily.title: Worrying
daily.description: Telling a friend that something keeps bothering you.
daily.example: The more I think about it, the more worried I get.

work.title: Asking for a quick reply
work.description: In business, hoping the other side answers soon.
work.example: The sooner you can reply, the better.

work.title: A rule of thumb
work.description: Explaining a principle in training or a report.
work.example: The more data you have, the more accurate the results.

etymology: A mix of the conditional 「〜ば」 and 「ほど（程）」 for degree. Literally “if ..., to the degree of ...”, which came to mean two things changing together: “the more ..., the more ...”.
formation: Combines the conditional 「〜ば」 with 「ほど（程）」 (degree), repeating the same word in between. 「考えれば考えるほど」 literally means “if you think, then to the degree you think ...”: 「ば」 first sets “thinking” as the condition, then 「ほど」 turns it into a sliding scale: however far the first goes, the second follows. The two thus rise and fall together in proportion: “the more ..., the more ...”. Because it describes continuous proportional change, the second part must be a state or evaluation that can vary, not a one-time event. When 「ば」 is dropped and only 「〜ほど」 remains, the scale is still there, just with a weaker sense of condition.

similar.title: 〜ほど (degree)
similar.explanation: Same origin: dropping 「〜ば」 and saying just 「〜ほど」 can also mean “the more ..., the more ...” (「年を取るほど体が弱くなる」), but the sense of condition is weaker and it's more written; 「ば〜ほど」 is the full form, common in both speech and writing.

similar.title: 〜につれて
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「につれて」 describes gradual change as time passes or things shift, and is more written (「時間が経つにつれて」); 「ば〜ほど」 stresses that two degrees are proportional and can state general rules (「多ければ多いほどいい」), where 「につれて」 can't be used.

similar.title: 〜にしたがって
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「にしたがって」 also means “as ...”, is even more formal than 「につれて」, and suits regular proportional change; 「ば〜ほど」 is the most colloquial and common way to say it.

similar.title: 〜ば (conditional)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the first half of this pattern is the conditional 「〜ば」. 「〜ば」 alone is just “if ..., then ...”; adding the repeated 「〜ほど」 turns the condition into a sliding “degree”, expressing change in step.

meaning: Concession, “even if … / even though …”: even when the first part holds (with verbs, adjectives or nouns), the second part is unaffected. Paired with a question word it means “no matter what / how / how much …,” and the result does not change.
connection: Verb て-form + も; い-adjective くて + も; na-adjective / noun + でも; question word (何・誰・どこ・いくら・どんなに etc.) + 〜ても

senses.label: Verbs: even if ...
senses.meaning: Supposes or admits something, but the result goes against expectations or stays the same: “even if ...”, “even though ...”.
senses.connection: Verb て-form + も (「降っても」, 「飲んでも」, 「行っても」)
examples: Even if it rains, the game will go ahead.
Even though I took medicine, my fever won't go down.
Even if we go now, we probably won't make it.

senses.label: Adjectives: even if ...
senses.meaning: With an adjective: no matter the quality, the result stays the same.
senses.connection: い-adjective く + ても; な-adjective + でも
examples: Even if it's expensive, I want to buy this book.
Even if the work is tough, I'll do my best.

senses.label: Nouns: even ...
senses.meaning: With a noun: “even (if it's) ...”, and the result doesn't change.
senses.connection: Noun + でも
examples: Even on Sundays, I have to go to the office.
Even a child understands this much.

senses.label: No matter what ...
senses.meaning: However the condition changes, the result is the same: “no matter what ...”. The result is often negative or disappointing.
senses.connection: 何を／誰に／どこへ／いつ + verb て-form + も
examples: No matter how many times I explain, he doesn't get it.
No matter who I asked, the answer was the same.
Wherever you go, it's crowded.

senses.label: No matter how much ...
senses.meaning: 「いくら〜ても」 and 「どんなに〜ても」 mean that even at a high degree, the result doesn't change: “no matter how ...”.
senses.connection: いくら／どんなに + verb て-form, い-adjective くて, な-adjective で + も
examples: No matter how much I eat, I don't gain weight.
No matter how busy I am, I eat breakfast.

senses.label: どうしても
senses.meaning: 「どうしても」 has two meanings: with a wish, “really want to ... no matter what”; with a negative, “just can't ...”.
senses.connection: どうしても + 〜たい／〜なければならない; どうしても + negative
examples: I really want to go to Japan, no matter what.
Whatever I try, I can't solve this problem.

notes: For a hypothetical concession, 「のに」 can't be used: ✕「明日雨が降るのに行きます」→ ○「明日雨が降っても行きます」. 「のに」 is only for facts that have already happened.
「ても」 and 「たら」 are opposites: 「雨が降っても行く」 (I'll go even if it rains) vs 「雨が降ったら行かない」 (if it rains, I won't go). Say 「たら」 instead of 「ても」 and the whole meaning changes.
Watch the te-form sound changes and adjective forms: ○「読んでも」「死んでも」; 「いい」 becomes 「よくても」 (✕「いいても」); nouns and な-adjectives use 「でも」 (✕「学生だでも」 ✕「静かくても」).
The question word must pair with 「ても」; switch to 「たら」 or 「ば」 and it becomes “if”: ✕「どこへ行ったら、人が多い」→ ○「どこへ行っても、人が多い」.
「何度言っても」 and 「いくら説明しても」 carry frustration (“no matter how often I say it, you don't listen”). Used with a superior or client, they sound accusatory; avoid them in business.

daily.title: Showing determination
daily.description: Telling a friend you're going no matter what.
daily.example: Even if I have a fever, I'm going to the concert tomorrow.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Cheering up a friend who's upset over something small.
daily.example: There's no use regretting it now.

daily.title: Talking about food
daily.description: Describing your eating habits.
daily.example: Even when I'm full, I can still eat sweets.

daily.title: Can't find something
daily.description: Searching the house for your keys.
daily.example: I've looked everywhere, but I can't find my keys.

daily.title: Talking about yourself
daily.description: Answering a friend who envies you.
daily.example: No matter how much I sleep, I'm still sleepy.

work.title: Announcing a rule
work.description: A company notice says the plan won't change.
work.example: Even if it rains, the event will be held as planned.

work.title: Reporting the situation
work.description: Telling your boss a problem hasn't been solved.
work.example: I've checked many times, but the data doesn't match.

work.title: Reporting a malfunction
work.description: Reporting a device problem to the IT team.
work.example: No matter how many times I restart it, I get an error.

work.title: Making a promise
work.description: Assuring a client you'll meet the deadline whatever happens.
work.example: No matter how busy we are, we'll always meet the deadline.

etymology: 「ても」 is the conjunctive particle 「て」 plus the focus particle 「も」. 「て」 links the two parts, and 「も」 adds the concessive tone “even so,” together meaning “even if … , still ….” With a question word in front, it means “whichever it is, still …,” a total concession.
formation: 「て」 attaches the first part as one situation (real or hypothetical), and 「も」 means “also / even”: “even if this is counted in, the conclusion is the same.” That is concession. Since 「も」 only says “adding it changes nothing” and does not distinguish real from hypothetical, it can express hypotheticals (「降っても行く」) as well as events that already happened (「飲んでも治らなかった」). Nouns and na-adjectives have no て-form of their own and borrow 「で」, the て-form of 「だ」, giving 「でも」. With a question word, the word stands for “any one (place, person, number of times, method),” extending the concession to every possibility so that only one unchanged conclusion remains; hence the second part is often “the result is the same” or a resigned “nothing works.” 「いくら」 and 「どんなに」 switch the questioned element to “degree, quantity,” giving “however much … , still ….”

similar.title: たとえ〜ても
similar.explanation: Same origin: adding the adverb 「たとえ」 stresses that it's a hypothesis, and an extreme one: “even if ..., still ...”, stronger than 「ても」 alone.

similar.title: いくら〜ても
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「いくら〜ても」 is a type of this pattern where the question is about amount or degree: “however much ..., still ...”, often with repeated actions (「いくら食べても太らない」).

similar.title: どんなに〜ても
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「どんなに〜ても」 is also a type of this pattern, stressing “no matter how ...”, especially common with adjectives (「どんなに忙しくても」).

similar.title: 〜としても
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「としても」 explicitly marks the first part as a supposition, “even supposing ...”, attaches to nouns and plain forms (「行くとしても」), and is more written; 「ても」 is common in both speech and writing.

meaning: In casual speech, lists a few examples and hints there are more, like “... and ... and stuff”, “things like ...”.
connection: Noun / verb or adjective plain form + とか (+ noun / plain form + とか)

senses.label: Listing nouns
senses.meaning: Gives some concrete examples: “like ...”, “... and ... and so on”. More casual than 「や〜など」.
senses.connection: Noun + とか + noun + とか (can be followed by 「が」, 「を」, 「に」)
examples: On days off, I go to the movies, go shopping, and so on.
As for fruit, I like apples, bananas and stuff.

senses.label: Listing actions
senses.meaning: After verbs or clauses, it lists actions or situations. You can also give just one, as a soft suggestion.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + とか (〜とか〜とか／〜とかしたら)
examples: On weekends I'm busy with housework, like cleaning and laundry.
You should talk to your teacher or something.

senses.label: Vague examples
senses.meaning: A single 「とか」 makes what you say vague and indirect, so it sounds relaxed. Common among young people.
senses.connection: Noun + とか
examples: Want some coffee or something?
Want to go to karaoke or something next time?

notes: 「とか」 is casual speech. In formal documents, business emails or explanations to clients, switch to 「〜や〜など」 or 「〜など」, or you'll sound flippant and unprofessional.
Tacking 「とか」 onto everything to avoid committing (「私とか、そう思うんですけど」) is a verbal tic of young people; at work or in interviews it sounds immature, so avoid it.
「〜とか」 at the end of a sentence is uncertain hearsay, “I heard ...”: 「彼、結婚したとか」 isn't a list but “I heard he got married”.
「何とか」 means “somehow, manage to”, not listing: 「何とか間に合った」 is “I somehow made it in time”.

daily.title: Talking about hobbies
daily.description: Chatting with a new friend about what you like to do.
daily.example: I like music, movies, that kind of thing.

daily.title: Shopping list
daily.description: Asking a family member to pick up some things.
daily.example: Could you get some milk and eggs and stuff?

daily.title: Giving a friend advice
daily.description: A friend isn't feeling well, and you make suggestions.
daily.example: Why not take some medicine, go to bed early, that sort of thing?

work.title: Casual discussion
work.description: Brainstorming ideas with coworkers.
work.example: How about advertising on social media, videos, that kind of thing?

etymology: Made of the quotation particle 「と」 plus the question particle 「か」. It first meant an uncertain “is it ... or ...?”. From that vague “maybe it's ...” tone, it came to be used for casual listing.
formation: 「とか」 consists of the quoting particle 「と」 and 「か」, which marks questions and uncertainty; its original sense is roughly “did someone say ...?”, with a noncommittal tone. Adding this uncertainty after each example gives “like ..., ..., and so on”: each example is offered without claiming it's the only one, implying there are others. With a single 「とか」, the uncertainty makes a statement vague and indirect, which gives the soft-example use. The original “quoting” sense of 「と」 survives at the end of a sentence as the hearsay “I heard ...”.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both list “... and ... etc.”, but 「や〜など」 only takes nouns and is more formal; 「とか」 can also take verbs and clauses and is very colloquial.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: for listing actions, 「〜たり〜たりする」 is the standard form; 「〜とか〜とか」 is more casual and can list both actions and nouns.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「やら〜やら」 also lists, but usually with an exclamatory “what with ... and ..., it's chaos” feel, often for negative or hectic situations.

similar.title: 〜とか (hearsay)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same 「とか」 at the end of a sentence marks uncertain hearsay, “I heard ...” (「明日は雨だとか」), unrelated to listing.

meaning: Shows that one kind of thing is abundant or keeps recurring, “nothing but ..., only ...”, often with a tone of dissatisfaction or criticism; after a quantity word it gives an approximate amount, “about ...”.
connection: Noun (+ particle) + ばかり; quantity word / 少し + ばかり

senses.label: Nothing but ...
senses.meaning: Almost all of something is the same thing, or the same action keeps happening: “nothing but”, “only”. Often with a complaint or criticism.
senses.connection: Noun + ばかり (+ verb)
examples: My little brother eats nothing but sweets.
It's been nothing but rain lately, hasn't it?
This class is all girls.

senses.label: After a particle
senses.meaning: To limit the target, 「ばかり」 can come after a particle: “only to ...”, “only in ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + に／と／で + ばかり
examples: My mom is only nice to my little sister.
He only thinks about himself.

senses.label: Casual ばっかり
senses.meaning: In speech it often becomes 「ばっかり」, which is stronger and more casual.
senses.connection: Noun + ばっかり
examples: Stop complaining all the time.
I play nothing but video games every day.

senses.label: About / around
senses.meaning: After words for amount, length of time, distance or money, it gives a rough figure: “about ...”. It is slightly more formal and old-fashioned than 「くらい」.
senses.connection: Number + counter + ばかり (十分ばかり・一週間ばかり・千円ばかり)
examples: I live about a ten-minute walk from the station.
I took about a week off.
Could you lend me about 1,000 yen?

senses.label: 少しばかり
senses.meaning: 「少しばかり」 means a small amount or degree: “a little, slightly”. When giving a gift, 「少しばかりですが」 is a humble phrase.
senses.connection: 少し + ばかり (+ ですが／の + noun)
examples: It's just a little something, but please accept it.
I'm a little tired today.

notes: 「ばかり」 often carries dissatisfaction or criticism, so using it about others sounds like blame: telling a manager 「部長は会議ばかりですね」 may be heard as a complaint. For a neutral “only”, use 「だけ」.
To limit to “just one, just a little”, use 「だけ」: ✕「一つばかりください」→ ○「一つだけください」. 「ばかり」 means “lots of, full of”.
「〜たばかり」 means “just did”, a completely different meaning: 「食べたばかり」 is “just ate”, while 「甘いものばかり食べる」 is “eat nothing but sweets”.
It follows only quantity words that express an “amount” (三日ばかり・千円ばかり), not points in time: ✕「三時ばかりに来て」 → ○「三時ごろに来て」.

The position of 「ばかり」 decides the meaning: 「一時間ばかり待った」 is “I waited about an hour,” 「待ってばかりいた」 is “all I did was wait,” and 「待ったばかりだ」 is “I have just finished waiting.” Put it in the wrong place and the meaning changes completely.

daily.title: A parent scolding a child
daily.description: A mom sees her child not eating vegetables.
daily.example: Don't eat only meat. Eat your vegetables too.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Small talk with a neighbor in the rainy season.
daily.example: It's been nothing but rainy days lately, so the laundry won't dry.

daily.title: Teasing a friend
daily.description: A friend keeps talking about the same thing.
daily.example: All you ever talk about is your boyfriend.

daily.title: Borrowing money
daily.description: Asking someone you know to lend you a little money.
daily.example: Sorry, but could you lend me about 2,000 yen?

daily.title: Giving a gift
daily.description: Handing over a small gift on a visit, with a humble phrase.
daily.example: It's just a little something, but please enjoy it together.

work.title: Complaining about work
work.description: Coworkers talk about what they've been doing lately.
work.example: Lately it's been nothing but meetings, so I can't get my own work done.

work.title: Asking your boss
work.description: Asking your boss to spare a little time.
work.example: Could I have about five minutes of your time?

etymology: 「ばかり」 comes from 「はかり」, the noun form of the verb 「はかる（計る・量る）」 (to measure), meaning “an estimate, a rough amount”. From this came the “about” meaning, and later the meanings “only, nothing but” and “just (done)”.
formation: 「ばかり」 comes from the nominalized continuative form 「はかり」 of the verb 「はかる（量る・計る）」, originally “the amount that was measured.” After an expression of quantity it means “the amount estimated by…,” hence “about, or so”; it is itself an estimate, not an exact figure. Because it is an “estimate of quantity,” it can follow only words of amount or duration, not points in time. 「少しばかり」 estimates “a small amount” once more and stresses “just a little,” so it is often used modestly. Later, from “measured only to this much” came “only, nothing but,” and from “the action’s amount has just reached this point” came “just now”; that is why these related uses look the same.

similar.title: 〜だけ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「だけ」 objectively limits to “only”, with no judgment; 「ばかり」 means “all, nothing but” and usually sounds dissatisfied. 「野菜だけ食べる」 is a plain statement, while 「野菜ばかり食べる」 implies “too one-sided”.

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「てばかりいる」 puts 「ばかり」 after a verb te-form, limiting the action: “always doing ...”; 「ゲームばかりしている」 and 「ゲームをしてばかりいる」 mean about the same.

similar.title: 〜ばかりで
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜ばかりで」 is followed by a negative or a negative evaluation: “only ... and never ...” (「文句を言うばかりで、何もしない」), an extension of the “nothing but” meaning.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい
similar.explanation: Similar in meaning; both express an approximate quantity. 〜くらい is the most common and colloquial; 〜ばかり feels slightly formal and a bit old-fashioned, and is less used in modern speech.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「ばかり」 after the ta-form means “just…” (来たばかり); after a quantity word it means “about.”

meaning: Someone keeps doing the same thing and nothing else. Usually sounds critical or annoyed.
connection: Verb て-form + ばかりいる

senses.label: Always doing ...
senses.meaning: Someone keeps doing one thing and neglects what they should do: “do nothing but ...”, “keep ...ing”. The speaker usually disapproves.
senses.connection: Verb て-form + ばかりいる／ばかりいた
examples: She's been crying since this morning.
My dad does nothing but sleep on his days off.
In my school days, all I did was play.

senses.label: Telling someone to stop
senses.meaning: 「〜てばかりいないで」 tells someone not to keep doing something. In speech, it's often 「〜てばっかり」.
senses.connection: Verb て-form + ばかりいないで + command / request
examples: Stop playing all the time and study.
Stop complaining and help me out.

notes: 「たばかり」 and 「てばかり」 differ by a single kana but mean completely different things: 「食べたばかり」 is “just ate”, 「食べてばかりいる」 is “does nothing but eat”.
「ばかり」 must go between the te-form and 「いる」: ✕「泣きばかりいる」; 「泣いているばかり」 means “just crying (doing nothing else)”, with a different nuance.
The critical tone is strong, so describing a superior or elder this way (✕「部長は電話してばかりいますね」) is very rude; about yourself, it's self-reflection and perfectly fine.
Different from 「〜ばかりだ」: 「悪くなるばかりだ」 takes the dictionary form and means a situation keeps getting worse, not “always doing something”.

daily.title: A mom to her child
daily.description: A mom talks to a child who's always on their phone.
daily.example: Stop staring at your phone and go to bed.

daily.title: Reflecting with a friend
daily.description: Talking about how you've been living lately.
daily.example: I've been doing nothing but eating lately, and I've gained weight.

work.title: A senior advising a junior
work.description: Telling a junior to take the initiative.
work.example: Don't keep relying on others. Try thinking it through yourself.

work.title: Reflecting in a meeting
work.description: A team looks back on why a problem happened.
work.example: We kept putting off the problem.

etymology: Made of a verb て-form, the particle 「ばかり」 (“nothing but”), and 「いる」 for an ongoing state: “being in a state of only doing this”.
formation: Built as verb te-form + 「ばかり」 + 「いる」. 「〜ている」 shows being in the middle of an ongoing action; inserting 「ばかり」 (“the whole extent falls on this”) between 「て」 and 「いる」 gives “the state one is in is entirely doing this”. 「ばかり」 itself implies “nothing else”, so the pattern carries criticism: “doing only this and not what one should”. Its position decides what 「ばかり」 limits: here, the action itself; placed after 「いる」 (「ているばかり」), it limits the state instead: “just being in that state”.

similar.title: 〜ばかり (nothing but)
similar.explanation: Same origin: noun + 「ばかり」 limits the object, “nothing but ...”; 「てばかりいる」 limits the action, “always doing ...”. 「ゲームばかりしている」≈「ゲームをしてばかりいる」.

similar.title: 〜ばかりで
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜ばかりで」 is followed by “and doesn't do ...”, making the criticism explicit (「遊ぶばかりで、勉強しない」); 「てばかりいる」 already implies “not doing what one should”.

similar.title: 〜てばかりはいられない
similar.explanation: Same origin: adding 「は」 after 「ばかり」 and using a negative potential gives “can't just keep ...”, meaning it's time to act (「泣いてばかりはいられない」).

meaning: Just one simple condition is enough to bring about the result; or only a certain means or range is used.
connection: Verb plain form / noun + だけで

senses.label: Just ... is enough to ...
senses.meaning: Nothing else is needed; this alone leads to the result: “just ...ing makes ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / た-form + だけで
examples: Just thinking about it makes me happy.
Just hearing his voice cheered me up.
Just by looking, you can tell if it's tasty.

senses.label: Only with ...
senses.meaning: After a noun, it means using only a certain means or ingredient, or only certain people: “with only ...”, “just ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + だけで
examples: This dish is seasoned with just salt.
I want to talk with just the two of us.

senses.label: All you need is ...
senses.meaning: 「〜だけでいい」 means doing just this is enough: “all you need to do is ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / noun + だけでいい (だけで大丈夫／だけで十分)
examples: All you need to do is write your name here.
The thought alone is plenty.

notes: 「だけで」 and 「だけでなく」 differ only slightly but mean completely different things: 「見るだけで分かる」 is “you can tell just by looking”, while 「見るだけでなく」 is “not only look, but also ...”.
「お気持ちだけで十分です」 and 「お気持ちだけいただきます」 are set phrases for politely declining a gift or treat: “I appreciate the thought, but there's no need”. They are not acceptance.
な-adjectives need 「な」: ✕「静かだけで」→ ○「静かなだけで」; nouns attach directly: 「名前だけで」.
「二人だけで」 means “just the two of us (no one else)”. Telling a colleague 「二人だけで話したい」 can make a third person feel excluded; at work, 「少しお時間よろしいですか」 is more appropriate.

daily.title: Looking forward to a trip
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about an upcoming trip.
daily.example: Just thinking about the trip gets me excited.

daily.title: Talking about health
daily.description: A friend asks how you lost weight.
daily.example: I lost three kilos just by walking every day.

daily.title: Getting a present
daily.description: Politely responding when a friend brings a gift.
daily.example: I'm happy just that you came.

work.title: Explaining how it works
work.description: Showing a client how handy some software is.
work.example: Just press this button, and the document is created.

work.title: Paperwork
work.description: A clerk tells a customer the procedure is simple.
work.example: All you need to do is sign here.

etymology: 「だけ」 comes from 「丈（たけ）」 with a voiced sound, originally “length, limit”, and later “only this much”. Add 「で」 for means or state, and you get “just by this”.
formation: Made of 「だけ」 (limit) and the case particle 「で」. 「だけ」 originally means “limit, only this range”, and 「で」 marks means, condition or state. 「Xだけで」 literally means “with only the range of X”. When the second part is a result, it means “nothing more is needed; X alone brings about ...”, stressing the contrast between a small condition and a big result (「考えるだけで楽しい」); when it's an action, the “means” sense of 「で」 comes forward: “do it using only X” (「塩だけで味をつける」). Followed by 「いい／十分」, it's “X alone is enough”, i.e. “all you need is ...”.

similar.title: 〜だけ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「だけ」 just limits the scope, “only”; adding 「で」 (means, condition) stresses “this alone is enough (for a result)” or “using only this means”.

similar.title: 〜さえ〜ば
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「さえ〜ば」 states the one necessary condition, “as long as ..., then ...”, more forcefully, ruling out all other conditions; 「だけでいい」 also means “you only need to do this”, but sounds milder.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: Same origin: adding the negative 「なく」 after 「だけで」 turns it into “not only ... but also ...”; 「だけで」 is “just ... is enough”. Only 「なく」 separates them, yet the meanings are completely different.

meaning: After a number, shows equal shares (“... each”) or repeating the same amount (“little by little”, “one at a time”).
connection: Number + counter / degree adverbs like 少し・ちょっと + ずつ

senses.label: Equal shares
senses.meaning: Each person or thing gets the same amount: “... each”, “... apiece”.
senses.connection: Number + counter + ずつ (often with 「一人に」 or 「それぞれ」)
examples: I gave everyone two apples each.
One red pen and one blue pen, please.

senses.label: One at a time
senses.meaning: Repeating with the same amount each time: “... at a time”, “one by one”.
senses.connection: 一 + counter + ずつ (「一つずつ」, 「一人ずつ」, 「一歩ずつ」)
examples: Let's check them one at a time.
When your name is called, please come in one at a time.

senses.label: Little by little
senses.meaning: 「少しずつ」 and 「ちょっとずつ」 mean doing or changing slowly and gradually.
senses.connection: 少し／ちょっと + ずつ
examples: I study a little Japanese every day.
The illness is getting better little by little.

notes: 「ずつ」 means each person or thing gets this amount, not the total: 「りんごを二つずつあげた」 is “gave two apples each”, not “gave two in total”.
The correct spelling is 「ずつ」; writing 「づつ」 counts as a mistake in exams and formal documents.
For “every other ... / at intervals of ...”, use 「おきに」 or 「ごとに」: ✕「三日ずつ薬を飲む」 (that means “three days each”) → ○「三日おきに薬を飲む」.
「ずつ」 attaches to specific amounts or to 「少し」「ちょっと」, but usually not to vague amounts like 「全部」 or 「たくさん」: ✕「全部ずつ」.

daily.title: Sharing snacks
daily.description: A mom hands out snacks to her kids.
daily.example: Three cookies each, okay?

daily.title: A study plan
daily.description: Telling a friend how you study.
daily.example: I learn ten words every day.

daily.title: Moving house
daily.description: Reminding each other while packing.
daily.example: Let's carry the boxes one at a time.

work.title: Instructions
work.description: How to take a medicine, from the label.
work.example: Take two tablets at a time, three times a day.

work.title: Assigning tasks
work.description: A team leader splits up the work.
work.example: Each of you three, please handle ten pages of this document.

etymology: 「ずつ」 is generally thought to come from the old form 「づつ」, meaning “each, in equal parts”. Some link it to the counter 「つ」. Modern kana rules write it 「ずつ」, though 「づつ」 shows up in older texts.
formation: 「ずつ」 is generally thought to come from the old form 「づつ」, which followed quantities and meant “each, apportioned by”; modern kana spelling standardizes it as 「ずつ」. The core of 「Xずつ」 is “with X as one unit, portion by portion”: handing this unit to several recipients gives equal sharing, “X for each”; repeating it over time gives “X at a time, one by one”; when the unit is 「少し」 or 「ちょっと」, it becomes “little by little”, gradual progress or change. Since 「ずつ」 is built on “a fixed unit”, it doesn't attach to words like 「全部」 or 「たくさん」 that can't serve as a unit.

similar.title: 〜ごとに
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「ごとに」 means “each ... separately” or “every ...” (「一時間ごとに」), focusing on repetition unit by unit; 「ずつ」 focuses on each recipient getting the same amount. 「一人ずつ」 is “one at a time”, 「一人ごとに」 is “for each person separately”.

similar.title: 〜当たり (per)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「一人当たり」 is a calculated average, “per person”, used for ratios and statistics; 「ずつ」 is an amount actually handed out or done step by step.

similar.title: 〜につき
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜につき」 can also express allocation per unit (「一人につき二枚」); it's used in rules and notices and is fairly formal. In speech you'd say 「一人二枚ずつ」.
